\chapter{Ways of Going}
\label{ch:hi-ways-of-going}
\hlchaptermodality{76}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name what carries me, ask for a ticket, and say that I am going somewhere.}

Complete HI-C69-go and say all five words in order, then say that you go to the station.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[gāṛī]{\hi{गाड़ी} (gāṛī) — a vehicle; a train}

\label{lesson:HI-C69-vehicle}



\begin{quote}
Two words back before anything new: what does \emph{bhāshā} mean, and what is \textbf{\hi{अंग्रेज़ी}}? The next five words are how you leave the \hi{शहर} you live in.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{गाड़ी}}
\textbf{\hi{गाड़ी}} (\emph{gāṛī}) — \textquotedblleft{}a vehicle\textquotedblright{}.

From Sanskrit \hi{गर्त} (\emph{garta}), a cart, through the Prakrits. It began as the thing oxen pulled and it has taken in everything since: a car is a \hi{गाड़ी}, a train is a \hi{गाड़ी}, a bullock cart is a \hi{गाड़ी}.

That width is the reason to learn it first. \textbf{\hi{बस}} you already own, and \hi{बस} names one thing only. \hi{गाड़ी} names whatever is carrying you, so it is the word that never leaves you stuck — point at anything with wheels and \hi{गाड़ी} is right.

The \hi{ड़} in the middle is the flapped retroflex, made by flicking the tongue down off the roof of the mouth. It is \hi{ड} with the nuqta underneath.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The first of five words for getting somewhere.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{bhāshā}, then read \textbf{\hi{अंग्रेज़ी}} and say what it means
  \item \emph{Hear:} \emph{gāṛī}, slowly, with the flap in the middle
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{gāṛī}
  \item \emph{Contrast:} \emph{gāṛī} and \emph{bas}, and say which one is wider
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \hi{गाड़ी} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a vehicle\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[rel]{\hi{रेल} (rel) — the railway}

\label{lesson:HI-C69-railway}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{gāṛī}, then write \textbf{\hi{गाड़ी}}: \hi{ग}, then the \hi{ा} stroke, then \hi{ड} with its nuqta, then \hi{ी}. Four pieces, all of them yours already.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{रेल}}
\textbf{\hi{रेल}} (\emph{rel}) — \textquotedblleft{}the railway\textquotedblright{}.

English \emph{rail}, borrowed whole in the nineteenth century and spelt with the \hi{े} matra, which is where an English \emph{ay} sound usually lands in Devanagari.

\hi{रेल} on its own is the system: the network, the line, the railway as an institution. The train itself is \textbf{\hi{रेलगाड़ी}} — \hi{रेल} plus the \hi{गाड़ी} you learnt in the last lesson — and in speech people shorten that back to plain \hi{गाड़ी}. Two words you now hold combine into the third without anything new.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
\hi{गाड़ी} and \hi{रेल}, and the compound they make between them.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} read \textbf{\hi{अंग्रेज़ी}}, then say it without looking
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{rel}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{rel}, then \emph{gāṛī}, then \emph{relgāṛī}
  \item \emph{Write it:} \hi{गाड़ी} once more, without looking
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \hi{रेल} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}the railway\textquotedblright{}.) What is a \hi{रेलगाड़ी}? (\textquotedblleft{}a train\textquotedblright{}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[sṭeshan]{\hi{स्टेशन} (sṭeshan) — a station}

\label{lesson:HI-C69-station}



\begin{quote}
Which of your two words names the network, and which names the thing that moves along it?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{स्टेशन}}
\textbf{\hi{स्टेशन}} (\emph{sṭeshan}) — \textquotedblleft{}a station\textquotedblright{}.

English \emph{station}, and it shows its seams. Hindi does not open a word with two consonants stuck together, so the writing does it the Devanagari way instead: \hi{स} with the vowel-killer \hi{्} underneath, then \hi{ट}. That stack is the same virama you met inside \hi{नमस्ते}.

The retroflex \hi{ट} rather than dental \hi{त} is deliberate. When Hindi borrows an English \emph{t}, it hears the English tongue as curled back, so \emph{station} becomes \hi{स्टेशन} and not \hi{स्तेशन}. Every English \emph{t} you meet in a Hindi loan will do this.

The word is painted on every platform board in the country, in Devanagari and in Latin letters side by side.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Three: \hi{गाड़ी}, \hi{रेल}, \hi{स्टेशन}. A vehicle, a network, and the place you wait.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Read it:} \hi{स्टेशन}, and find the \hi{्} that stacks the first two letters
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{sṭeshan}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{rel sṭeshan}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \hi{स्टेशन} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a station\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ṭikaṭ]{\hi{टिकट} (ṭikaṭ) — a ticket}

\label{lesson:HI-C69-ticket}



\begin{quote}
Write \textbf{\hi{स्टेशन}} from memory. Start with the stacked \hi{स्}, then \hi{ट}, then \hi{े} on top, then \hi{श}, then \hi{न}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{टिकट}}
\textbf{\hi{टिकट}} (\emph{ṭikaṭ}) — \textquotedblleft{}a ticket\textquotedblright{}.

English \emph{ticket}, and both of its \emph{t} sounds land on retroflex \hi{ट} for the reason the last lesson gave. The \hi{ि} in the middle is the short \emph{i} matra, and it is written \textbf{before} the letter it is sounded after — you learnt that trick when you first wrote a name.

This is the word you actually say at a window. You already know how to ask for one thing politely: \textbf{\hi{एक} \hi{चाय} \hi{दीजिए}} got you a cup of tea. \textbf{\hi{एक} \hi{टिकट} \hi{दीजिए}} is the same frame with a new word dropped in, and it will get you onto a train.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Four, and a request you can already make with the fourth.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{ṭikaṭ}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{ek ṭikaṭ dījie}
  \item \emph{Write it:} \hi{टिकट}, putting the \hi{ि} down before the \hi{ट} it belongs to
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How do you ask for one ticket? (\emph{ek ṭikaṭ dījie}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[jānā]{\hi{जाना} (jānā) — to go}

\label{lesson:HI-C69-go}



\begin{quote}
Name the four words of this chapter so far.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{जाना}}
\textbf{\hi{जाना}} (\emph{jānā}) — \textquotedblleft{}to go\textquotedblright{}.

Sanskrit \hi{या} (\emph{yā-}), \textquotedblleft{}to go\textquotedblright{}, is the root; Hindi turned the initial \emph{y-} into \emph{j-}, which it does to many inherited words, and added the \textbf{-\hi{ना}} ending that every Hindi doing word carries when you name it plain.

You already own three that end the same way: \textbf{\hi{बोलना}}, \textbf{\hi{देखना}}, \textbf{\hi{सुनना}}. The ending is the pattern, not a coincidence, and \hi{जाना} now joins them.

\hi{जाना} is the one doing word a traveller cannot do without. \textbf{\hi{मैं} \hi{स्टेशन} \hi{जाता} \hi{हूँ}} uses the same shape as \textbf{\hi{मैं} \hi{हिंदी} \hi{बोलता} \hi{हूँ}}, which you have been saying since the early chapters — the same frame, a different word inside it.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Five: \hi{गाड़ी}, \hi{रेल}, \hi{स्टेशन}, \hi{टिकट}, \hi{जाना}. A way to travel and a way to say you are going.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{jānā}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{maiṁ sṭeshan jātā hūṁ}
  \item \emph{Write it:} \hi{टिकट} and then \hi{जाना}, both from memory
  \item \emph{Say it:} all five in order
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \hi{जाना} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}to go\textquotedblright{}.) Say that you go to the station.
\end{tcolorbox}
